title: Pair Sum Count
statement: You get a list of integers and a target value k. Count the pairs of positions (i, j) with i < j whose values add up to k. Two positions with equal values are different pairs.
input_format: First line: n and k. Second line: n integers.
output_format: One integer: the number of pairs.
idea: For each value, you only need to know how many earlier values complete it to k. Keep counts of values seen so far in a hash map and add the count of k - x as you go.
naive: Checking every pair takes about n squared steps, which is far too slow at n = 200000.
hints: For a fixed element, what single value would complete the pair?
Could you find out how many times that value has appeared earlier without scanning for it?
A hash map from value to count answers that in constant time on average.

complexity.time_why: One pass; each step does a constant-time average lookup and update.
complexity.space_why: The map can hold one entry per distinct value.

mistakes: Using a 32-bit integer for the count when it can reach about n squared over 2.
Counting a pair twice by looking both before and after the current element.

enforce.space_reason: Fixture only; no input size makes a quadratic-space approach fail without huge inputs.

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the hash-map solution?
quiz.explanation: One pass with constant-time average lookups.

quiz.q: What is the extra space of the hash-map solution?
quiz.explanation: The map stores up to one entry per distinct value.

quiz.q: What does a hash-map lookup cost on average?
quiz.explanation: With a good hash function the expected cost per lookup is constant.

quiz.q: All n values are equal and 2 * value equals k. Which integer type holds the answer safely?
quiz.explanation: The count reaches n * (n - 1) / 2, which can exceed 32 bits.

clarifications.answer: Values can repeat. Pairs are counted by position, not by value.

nudges: For one element, what value would complete the pair?
How can you know how many times that value appeared before, without a second loop?

followup.question: What changes if the array is sorted?
followup.discussion: Two pointers work in O(n) time and O(1) extra space; with many duplicates you count runs of equal values.

walkthrough.text: A hash map counts the values seen so far. The running count of pairs starts at zero.
For the current value x, the value that completes the pair is k - x. If it was seen before, every earlier copy forms a pair with x.
Only after counting do we record x, so an element never pairs with itself.
The count is a 64-bit integer because it can reach about n squared over two.
